judged_text: Both computed keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]" (Zod schemas have no custom toString) and the duplicate's second definition wins, so minimumTokenResponseSchema is effectively {access_token: z.string()} plus an optional "[object Object]" field and the expiry-number validation the comment describes does not exist. When credential sharing is enabled, any sync response containing only an access_token string passes validation and z.object strips all other fields, so the response's expiry is discarded — Office365 credentials keep a stale expiry_date and re-hit the sync endpoint on every calendar operation, and a malformed endpoint response is accepted silently.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` defines computed keys as `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. Since `z.string()` returns a Zod schema object and has no special `toString`, both computed keys become the literal string `"[object Object]"`, and the second definition overwrites the first. As a result, the intended "any numeric field is an expiry" validation does not exist; the schema effectively only requires `access_token` (and at most an optional `"[object Object]"` field). When credential sharing is enabled (`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` + `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`), `parseRefreshTokenResponse` uses this broken schema, so responses with only `access_token` will validate and any actual expiry fields will be dropped by `z.object`'s default stripping behavior, leading to stale expiry handling downstream (e.g., Office365 uses `tokenResponse.data` spread into existing credentials).
